summary: Details the IETF's policies on rights in contributions to the IETF. They are designed so that contributions can be made available to the IETF and the Internet community while letting authors retain as many rights as possible. It updates RFC 2026 and, with RFC 3668, replaced its section 10. It has been replaced by RFC 3978.

eli5.summary: When you share a drawing with a club, who owns it? This is the club's rule book on what rights authors keep and what the club may do. RFC 3978 later replaced it.

questions: what rights do ietf contributors grant
do authors keep copyright in rfcs
subtitle: The IETF's rulebook for what rights authors give away, and keep, when they submit a document.

tldr.problem: People who submit documents to the IETF automatically hold copyright and other rights, and RFC 2026's Section 10 on this had become the subject of vigorous debate over its exact intent.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3667 spells out the limited, non-exclusive rights every Contributor grants to the IETF and ISOC, the assurances they give, and the notices every IETF document must carry.
tldr.outcome: It is Best Current Practice 78, updated RFC 2026 and, with RFC 3668, replaced Section 10 of RFC 2026. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 3978.

today: RFC 3667 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 78) that updated RFC 2026, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 3978. Read RFC 3978 for the current rules.

sections.title: Why the Rules Were Written Down
sections.content:
Under the laws of most countries and international treaties such as the Berne Convention, authors get copyrights, moral rights and other rights automatically when they produce a work. If the work is made as part of a job, many of those rights usually go to the employer.

The IETF needs certain limited rights to publish and develop documents. These had been laid out in Section 10 of RFC 2026, but the exact intent of that section had been the subject of vigorous debate. RFC 3667 clarifies the ambiguities. It is not meant to substantially change current policy, and the RFC says it is not legal advice.

A companion document, RFC 3668, covers rights in technologies developed in the IETF Standards Process, which this document does not address.
sections.eli5: Anyone who makes something owns it from the moment they make it. The IETF club just needs a few clear permissions so it can share what people send in.

sections.title: Key Definitions
sections.content:
An IETF Contribution is any submission meant to become all or part of an Internet-Draft or RFC, plus any statement made within an IETF activity. That includes spoken remarks in IETF sessions and written messages to the plenary, working groups, the IESG, the IAB, IETF mailing lists, the RFC Editor or the Internet-Drafts function. Statements clearly not intended as input to an IETF activity are not Contributions.

An RFC Editor Contribution is an Internet-Draft meant for publication as an Informational or Experimental RFC but not as part of the IETF Standards Process. A Contributor is an individual submitting a Contribution. Internet-Drafts are temporary documents with a nominal maximum lifetime of 6 months in the Secretariat's public directory.

The phrase reasonably and personally known means what an individual knows personally or would reasonably be expected to know because of their job. It does not require anyone to run a patent search.
sections.eli5: Anything you say or send to the club on purpose counts as a contribution. You only have to tell the club about things you actually know, not go hunting for secrets.

sections.title: Rights Granted by Contributors
sections.content:
By submitting a Contribution, the submitter and each named co-Contributor, on behalf of any organization they represent or are sponsored by, are deemed to grant the ISOC and the IETF a perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive, royalty-free, world-wide license. It lets them copy, publish, display and distribute the Contribution in the IETF Standards Process or an Internet-Draft, allow translations into other languages, and reproduce trademarks included in it. Unless the notices forbid it, they may also prepare derivative works within the IETF Standards Process. Executable code in IETF Documents, such as MIB modules, may be extracted and reused for any purpose.

Contributors also give assurances, to the best of their knowledge and ability. They acknowledge all major Contributors, state that nothing in the Contribution is confidential, that nothing limits their ability to make the grants, that nothing included is intentionally defamatory, untrue or illegal where they live or work, and that trademarks are designated as such. Confidential material may not be submitted at all, and the IETF has no duty to publish anything.

RFC Editor Contributions follow a lighter version. They must meet Sections 3.1, 3.2, 3.4, 3.5 and 3.6, and the license covers publication as an RFC, translations, and derivative works unless disallowed, for at least the life of the Internet-Draft.
sections.eli5: When you send something in, you say the club may copy and share it forever, and you promise it is really yours to share. You still own it, and the club is not forced to use it.

sections.title: Notices Every IETF Document Carries
sections.content:
Certain notices must be reproduced verbatim in all IETF Documents, including copies, derivative works and translations. They protect the IETF and its participants from liability and tell readers that ISOC claims rights in layout, the RFC numbering convention and the prefatory language. The copyright legend does not mean ISOC owns the Contribution itself, which stays with the authors or remains in the public domain.

A Contributor who wants to take away the IETF's right to make derivative works (other than translations) may include one of two Derivative Works Limitation notices. These may not be used with standards-track documents or most working group documents. A Contributor who only wants an Internet-Draft, not an RFC, may add This document may only be posted in an Internet-Draft. Abbreviated notices are allowed for extractable material such as MIB modules.
sections.eli5: Every document gets the same small label saying who may do what with it. If an author wants to say do not change this, there is a special label for that too.

sections.title: Why the Procedures Look This Way
sections.content:
The main goal is to take from authors only the non-exclusive rights needed to develop and publish IETF Documents, and leave every other right with them. The rights the IETF needs are the right to publish, to let the document be reproduced in its published formats, to let third parties translate it, to make derivative works within the IETF process, and to let third parties extract logical parts such as MIB modules.

The IETF needs derivative works so it can evolve its documents based on deployment experience. The right is required for all standards-track documents and most others. Two exceptions exist: documents describing proprietary technologies, and republications of other standards organizations' work. The right to make translations is required before any Contribution can be published as an RFC.

Trademark licenses cover only reproducing, publishing and modifying the Contribution, and do not let anyone use a mark for a product or service. Even documents not subject to copyright, such as those from the U.S. government, are asked to carry the same grants and assurances.
sections.eli5: The club only asks for the permissions it truly needs. It wants to be able to improve a document over time, unless the author has a good reason, like a company that does not want others to rewrite its own design.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it relates to IETF process, not to any particular technology. It notes that adopting any technology carries security considerations, but that there are no known security issues with IETF Contribution rights policies.
sections.eli5: This is a rule book about paperwork, not about locks, so it says there is nothing dangerous in it.
